claim: The retina transforms patterns of light into visual feature representations supporting behaviour.
source: The retina transforms patterns of light into visual feature representations supporting behaviour.
evidence: This is a general statement about retinal function that draws from established scientific consensus.

claim: Visual feature representations are distributed across various types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs).
source: These representations are distributed across various types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), whose spatial and temporal tuning properties have been studied extensively in many model organisms, including the mouse.
evidence: This statement draws from established scientific knowledge about retinal organization.

claim: The spatial and temporal tuning properties of RGCs have been studied extensively in many model organisms, including the mouse.
source: These representations are distributed across various types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), whose spatial and temporal tuning properties have been studied extensively in many model organisms, including the mouse.
evidence: This is supported by references to prior research in the field.

claim: A convolutional neural network (CNN) model was trained on large-scale functional recordings of RGC responses to natural mouse movies.
source: We trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) model on large-scale functional recordings of RGC responses to natural mouse movies
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology used in the study.

claim: The CNN model was used to search in silico for stimuli that maximally excite distinct types of RGCs.
source: We trained a convolutional neural network (CNN) model on large-scale functional recordings of RGC responses to natural mouse movies, and then used this model to search in silico for stimuli that maximally excite distinct types of RGCs.
evidence: This describes the computational approach used in the study.

claim: The CNN model predicted centre colour opponency in transient suppressed-by-contrast (tSbC) RGCs.
source: This procedure predicted centre colour opponency in transient suppressed-by-contrast (tSbC) RGCs, a cell type whose function is being debated.
evidence: This is a prediction made by the computational model based on the data.

claim: The function of tSbC RGCs is being debated.
source: This procedure predicted centre colour opponency in transient suppressed-by-contrast (tSbC) RGCs, a cell type whose function is being debated.
evidence: This refers to the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: tSbC cells responded very selectively to Green-OFF, UV-ON contrasts.
source: We confirmed experimentally that these cells indeed responded very selectively to Green-OFF, UV-ON contrasts.
evidence: This is supported by experimental validation described in the manuscript.

claim: Green-OFF, UV-ON chromatic contrast is characteristic of transitions from ground to sky in the visual scene.
source: This type of chromatic contrast was characteristic of transitions from ground to sky in the visual scene, as might be elicited by head or eye movements across the horizon.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of natural scene statistics and cited literature.

claim: tSbC cells performed best among all RGC types at reliably detecting ground-to-sky transitions.
source: Because tSbC cells performed best among all RGC types at reliably detecting these transitions, we suggest a role for this RGC type in providing contextual information (i.e. sky or ground) necessary for the selection of appropriate behavioural responses to other stimuli, such as looming objects.
evidence: This is supported by the ROC analysis performed on the data.

claim: tSbC RGCs may provide contextual information (sky or ground) necessary for the selection of appropriate behavioural responses to other stimuli, such as looming objects.
source: Because tSbC cells performed best among all RGC types at reliably detecting these transitions, we suggest a role for this RGC type in providing contextual information (i.e. sky or ground) necessary for the selection of appropriate behavioural responses to other stimuli, such as looming objects.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Sensory systems evolved to generate representations of an animal's natural environment useful for survival and procreation.
source: Sensory systems evolved to generate representations of an animal's natural environment useful for survival and procreation (Lettvin et al., 1959).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work and represents established theory.

claim: Different features are relevant for different species.
source: These environments are complex and high dimensional, and different features are relevant for different species (reviewed in Baden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Features of the world relevant for the animal are represented with enhanced precision, whereas less important features are discarded.
source: As a consequence, the representations are adapted to an animal's needs: features of the world relevant for the animal are represented with enhanced precision, whereas less important features are discarded.
evidence: This is a general principle in sensory neuroscience supported by established knowledge.

claim: The visual system is well suited for studying sensory processing because the first features are already extracted at its experimentally well-accessible front-end, the retina.
source: The visual system is well suited for studying sensory processing, as the first features are already extracted at its experimentally well-accessible front-end, the retina (reviewed in Kerschensteiner, 2022; Baden et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles.

claim: In the mouse, the retina gives rise to around 40 parallel channels that detect different features.
source: In the mouse, this tissue gives rise to around 40 parallel channels that detect different features (Goetz et al., 2022; Baden et al., 2016; Bae et al., 2018; Rheaume et al., 2018)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Different types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs) represent different features, and their axons send information to numerous visual centres in the brain.
source: In the mouse, this tissue gives rise to around 40 parallel channels that detect different features (Goetz et al., 2022; Baden et al., 2016; Bae et al., 2018; Rheaume et al., 2018), represented by different types of retinal ganglion cells (RGCs), whose axons send information to numerous visual centres in the brain (Martersteck et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some retinal channels encode basic features, such as luminance changes and motion, that are only combined in downstream areas to support a range of behaviours such as cricket hunting in mice.
source: Some of these channels encode basic features, such as luminance changes and motion, that are only combined in downstream areas to support a range of behaviours such as cricket hunting in mice (Johnson et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Other retinal channels directly extract specific features from natural scenes necessary for specific behaviours.
source: Other channels directly extract specific features from natural scenes necessary for specific behaviours.
evidence: This is supported by the example provided and citations.

claim: Transient OFF α cells trigger freezing or escape behaviour in response to looming stimuli.
source: For instance, transient OFF α cells trigger freezing or escape behaviour in response to looming stimuli (Münch et al., 2009; Yilmaz and Meister, 2013; Kim et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: For many RGC types, we lack an understanding of the features they encode and how these link to behaviour.
source: For many RGC types, however, we lack an understanding of the features they encode and how these link to behaviour (Schwartz and Swygart, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Synthetic stimuli commonly used to study retinal processing fail to drive retinal circuits 'properly' and cannot uncover critical response properties triggered in natural environments.
source: One reason for this is that the synthetic stimuli commonly used to study retinal processing fail to drive retinal circuits 'properly' and, hence, cannot uncover critical response properties triggered in natural environments.
evidence: This is supported by the example provided and citation.

claim: Spatial nonlinear processing was found to be more complex for natural scenes than for simpler synthetic stimuli.
source: This was recently illustrated at the example of spatial nonlinear processing, which was found to be more complex for natural scenes than for simpler synthetic stimuli (Karamanlis and Gollisch, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Nonlinearities crucial for the encoding of natural stimuli cannot be captured by linear-nonlinear (LN) models of retinal processing.
source: Such nonlinearities, which are crucial for the encoding of natural stimuli, cannot be captured by linear-nonlinear (LN) models of retinal processing, and several alternative methods have been proposed for the analysis of natural stimulus responses (reviewed in Sharpee, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: Training a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict neuronal responses is one approach to modelling nonlinear visual processing.
source: One approach to modelling nonlinear visual processing is to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to predict neuronal responses.
evidence: This describes a methodological approach used in the field.

claim: The CNN approach has gained popularity in recent years, both in the retina and in higher visual areas.
source: This approach has gained popularity in recent years, both in the retina (McIntosh et al., 2016; Maheswaranathan et al., 2023; Tanaka et al., 2019; Batty et al., 2017) and in higher visual areas (Yamins et al., 2014; Cadena et al., 2019; Ustyuzhaninov et al., 2024).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: CNN models offer analysis techniques that have been used to investigate the contributions of different interneurons to a cell's response.
source: The resulting models, also referred to as 'digital twins', offer a number of analysis techniques that have been used to investigate, for example, the contributions of different interneurons to a cell's response (Maheswaranathan et al., 2023)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: CNN models have been used to investigate the effects of stimulus context on neural coding.
source: The resulting models, also referred to as 'digital twins', offer a number of analysis techniques that have been used to investigate, for example, the contributions of different interneurons to a cell's response (Maheswaranathan et al., 2023), or the effects of stimulus context (Fu et al., 2024; Goldin et al., 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: CNN models have been used to investigate the effects of behavioural state on neural coding.
source: The resulting models, also referred to as 'digital twins', offer a number of analysis techniques that have been used to investigate, for example, the contributions of different interneurons to a cell's response (Maheswaranathan et al., 2023), or the effects of stimulus context (Fu et al., 2024; Goldin et al., 2022) and behavioural state (Franke et al., 2022) on neural coding.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Feature visualisations can be used to quickly generate stimuli that would maximally excite the modelled neurons.
source: In particular, feature visualisations (Olah et al., 2017) can be used to quickly generate stimuli that would maximally excite the modelled neurons (Walker et al., 2019; Bashivan et al., 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Maximally exciting inputs (MEIs) can serve as interpretable short-hand descriptions of nonlinear neuronal selectivities.
source: In particular, feature visualisations (Olah et al., 2017) can be used to quickly generate stimuli that would maximally excite the modelled neurons (Walker et al., 2019; Bashivan et al., 2019), which in turn can serve as interpretable short-hand descriptions of nonlinear neuronal selectivities.
evidence: This is supported by citations and represents an inference about the utility of MEIs.

claim: In visual cortex, MEIs revealed more complex and diverse neuronal selectivities than were expected based on previous results obtained with synthetic stimuli and linear methods.
source: In visual cortex, the resulting maximally exciting inputs (MEIs) revealed more complex and diverse neuronal selectivities than were expected based on previous results obtained with synthetic stimuli and linear methods (Walker et al., 2019; Bashivan et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Colour is a salient feature in nature.
source: Colour is a salient feature in nature, and the mouse visual system dedicates intricate circuitry to the processing of chromatic information (Szél et al., 1992; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Baden et al., 2013; Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Mouland et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a general statement supported by citations.

claim: The mouse visual system dedicates intricate circuitry to the processing of chromatic information.
source: Colour is a salient feature in nature, and the mouse visual system dedicates intricate circuitry to the processing of chromatic information (Szél et al., 1992; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Baden et al., 2013; Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Mouland et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Studies using simple synthetic stimuli have revealed nonlinear and centre-surround (spatial) interactions between colour channels.
source: Studies using simple synthetic stimuli have revealed nonlinear and centre-surround (i.e. spatial) interactions between colour channels, but it is not clear how these are engaged in retinal processing of natural, temporally varying environments.
evidence: This is supported by the context and citations in the manuscript.

claim: It is not clear how nonlinear and centre-surround interactions between colour channels are engaged in retinal processing of natural, temporally varying environments.
source: Studies using simple synthetic stimuli have revealed nonlinear and centre-surround (i.e. spatial) interactions between colour channels, but it is not clear how these are engaged in retinal processing of natural, temporally varying environments.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Mouse photoreceptors are sensitive to green and UV light.
source: Since mouse photoreceptors are sensitive to green and UV light (Jacobs et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: RGC responses were recorded to stimuli capturing the chromatic composition of natural mouse environments in green and UV chromatic channels.
source: Since mouse photoreceptors are sensitive to green and UV light (Jacobs et al., 2004), we recorded RGC responses to stimuli capturing the chromatic composition of natural mouse environments in these two chromatic channels.
evidence: This describes the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: A model-guided search for MEIs in chromatic stimulus space predicted a novel type of chromatic tuning in tSbC RGCs.
source: A model-guided search for MEIs in chromatic stimulus space predicted a novel type of chromatic tuning in tSbC RGCs, a type whose function is being debated (Mani and Schwartz, 2017; Tien et al., 2015; Tien et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on computational modeling.

claim: A detailed in silico characterisation followed up by experimental validation ex-vivo confirmed tSbC cell type's pronounced and unique selectivity for dynamic full-field changes from green-dominated to UV-dominated scenes.
source: A detailed in silico characterisation followed up by experimental validation ex-vivo confirmed this cell type's pronounced and unique selectivity for dynamic full-field changes from green-dominated to UV-dominated scenes
evidence: This is supported by both computational and experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Dynamic full-field changes from green-dominated to UV-dominated scenes match the scene statistics of transitions across the horizon.
source: A detailed in silico characterisation followed up by experimental validation ex-vivo confirmed this cell type's pronounced and unique selectivity for dynamic full-field changes from green-dominated to UV-dominated scenes, a type of visual input that matches the scene statistics of transitions across the horizon (Qiu et al., 2021; Abballe and Asari, 2022; Gupta et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on natural scene statistics.

claim: tSbC RGCs may play a role in detecting behaviourally relevant changes in visual context, such as transitions from ground to sky.
source: We therefore suggest a role for tSbC RGCs in detecting behaviourally relevant changes in visual context, such as a transitions from ground (i.e. below the horizon) to sky (i.e. above the horizon).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: 8388 cells were recorded in 72 recording fields across 32 retinae in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) of the isolated mouse retina using two-photon population Ca2+ imaging.
source: Using two-photon population Ca2+ imaging, we recorded responses from 8388 cells (in 72 recording fields across 32 retinae) in the ganglion cell layer (GCL) of the isolated mouse retina (Figure 1a) to a range of visual stimuli.
evidence: This describes the experimental data collected.

claim: Complex interactions between colour channels have been mostly reported in the ventral retina and opsin-transitional zone.
source: Since complex interactions between colour channels have been mostly reported in the ventral retina and opsin-transitional zone, we focused our recordings on these regions (Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The recordings were focused on the ventral retina and opsin-transitional zone.
source: Since complex interactions between colour channels have been mostly reported in the ventral retina and opsin-transitional zone, we focused our recordings on these regions (Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021).
evidence: This describes the experimental design choice.

claim: 113 different movie clips were used, each lasting 5 s, displayed in pseudo-random order.
source: We used 113 different movie clips, each lasting 5 s, that were displayed in pseudo-random order.
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol.

claim: Five movie clips constituted the test set and were repeated three times to assess the reliability of neuronal responses across the recording.
source: Five of these constituted the test set and were repeated three times: at the beginning, in the middle, and at the end of the movie presentation, thereby allowing to assess the reliability of neuronal responses across the recording (Figure 1b, top).
evidence: This describes the experimental design for assessing response reliability.

claim: The responses elicited by the synthetic stimuli and the natural movie were diverse, displaying ON, ON-OFF, and OFF, as well as sustained and transient characteristics.
source: The responses elicited by the synthetic stimuli and the natural movie were diverse, displaying ON (Figure 1d, rows 4–9), ON-OFF (row 3), and OFF (rows 1 and 2), as well as sustained and transient characteristics (e.g. rows 8 and 4, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: Some responses were suppressed by temporal contrast.
source: Some responses were suppressed by temporal contrast (generally, rows 10, 11; at high contrast and frequency, row 9).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 6984 GCL cells passed the response quality criteria.
source: A total of 6984 GCL cells passed our response quality criteria (see Methods)
evidence: This describes the data after quality filtering.

claim: 3527 cells could be assigned to 1 of 32 previously characterised functional RGC groups based on their responses to the chirp and MB stimuli.
source: 3527 cells could be assigned to 1 of 32 previously characterised functional RGC groups (Baden et al., 2016) based on their responses to the chirp and MB stimuli using our recently developed classifier (Figure 1e; Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Qiu et al., 2021).
evidence: This describes the classification of cells based on their functional responses.

claim: The CNN model achieved an average test set correlation of 0.48 for all N=3527 cells passing filtering steps 1–3.
source: The mean correlation per RGC group ranged from 0.32 (G14) to 0.79 (G24) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and reached an average of 0.48 (for all N=3527 cells passing filtering steps 1–3, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This describes the performance of the CNN model on the test data.

claim: The nonlinear CNN model achieved a higher test set correlation than the LN model for all RGC groups.
source: We also tested the performance of our nonlinear model against a linearised version (see Methods; equivalent to an LN model, and from here on 'LN model') and found that the nonlinear CNN model achieved a higher test set correlation for all RGC groups (average correlation LN model: 0.38; G14: 0.2, G24: 0.65, Figure 2c).
evidence: This compares the performance of the nonlinear CNN model to a linear baseline.

claim: MEIs were short, dichromatic movie clips.
source: The resulting MEIs were short, dichromatic movie clips
evidence: This describes the output of the MEI generation procedure.

claim: MEIs of G20 (ON high frequency) had high average temporal frequency.
source: The MEI's temporal frequency relates to the temporal frequency preference of an RGC: MEIs of G20 and G21, termed ON high frequency and ON low frequency (Baden et al., 2016), had high and low average temporal frequency, respectively (G20, N=40 cells, green, mean ± SD: 2.71 ±0.16 Hz, UV 2.86 ±0.22 Hz
evidence: This is supported by the MEI analysis and is consistent with prior knowledge about G20 cells.

claim: MEIs of G21 (ON low frequency) had low average temporal frequency.
source: The MEI's temporal frequency relates to the temporal frequency preference of an RGC: MEIs of G20 and G21, termed ON high frequency and ON low frequency (Baden et al., 2016), had high and low average temporal frequency, respectively (G20, N=40 cells, green, mean ± SD: 2.71 ±0.16 Hz, UV 2.86 ±0.22 Hz; G21, N=50 cells, green, mean ± SD: 2.32 ±0.63 Hz, UV 1.98 ± 0.5 Hz; see Figure 3h).
evidence: This is supported by the MEI analysis and is consistent with prior knowledge about G21 cells.

claim: MEIs of ON and OFF RGCs had positive and negative contrasts, respectively.
source: Finally, the contrast of an MEI reflects what is traditionally called a cell's ON vs. OFF preference: MEIs of ON and OFF RGCs had positive and negative contrasts, respectively (Figure 3i).
evidence: This is supported by the MEI analysis.

claim: MEIs were largely consistent within functional RGC groups.
source: MEIs were also largely consistent within functional RGC groups (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 66% (24/36) of all G28 cells had colour-opponent MEIs (UVON-greenOFF).
source: Here, G28 stood out: 66% (24/36) of all cells of this group had colour-opponent MEIs (UVON-greenOFF), followed by G27 with 42% colour-opponent MEIs.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the MEI analysis.

claim: The colour opponency found in G28 was not centre-surround, but rather a centre opponency ('co-extensive' colour-opponent RF).
source: The colour opponency we found in G28 was not centre-surround, as described before in mice (Szatko et al., 2020), but rather a centre opponency ('co-extensive' colour-opponent RF; reviewed in Schwartz, 2021), as can be seen in the lower-dimensional visualisations (Figure 3a and b, right column; Figure 3c, orange trajectory).
evidence: This is supported by the MEI visualizations and contrasts with prior findings.

claim: The model-guided in silico exploration of chromatic stimulus space revealed a preference of G28 RGCs for centre colour-opponent, UVON-greenOFF stimuli, a feature previously unknown for this RGC group.
source: In conclusion, our model-guided in silico exploration of chromatic stimulus space revealed a variety of preferred stimuli that captured known properties of RGC groups, and revealed a preference of G28 RGCs for centre colour-opponent, UVON-greenOFF stimuli, a feature previously unknown for this RGC group.
evidence: This is a key finding of the study based on computational modeling.

claim: Most RGC groups exhibited their strongest or second-strongest response to their own group's MEI.
source: Indeed, most RGC groups exhibited their strongest (G5,20,21,28,32) or second-strongest (G1,10,23) response to their own group's MEI (Figure 4g, top).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation data shown in Figure 4g.

claim: RGC groups from opposing regions in response space showed no response to each others' MEIs.
source: Conversely, RGC groups from opposing regions in response space showed no response to each others' MEIs (e.g. G1,5 [OFF cells] vs. G21-28 [slow ON cells]).
evidence: This is supported by the experimental validation data.

claim: The model's predictions of MEI responses showed a similar pattern to the experimental data.
source: The model's predictions showed a similar pattern (Figure 4g, bottom), thereby validating the model's ability to generalise to the MEI stimulus regime.
evidence: This validates the model by comparing its predictions to experimental data.

claim: The validation experiments confirm the model's prediction that RGC group G28 is selective for centre colour-opponent, UVON-greenOFF stimuli.
source: Hence, our validation experiments confirm the model's prediction that RGC group G28 is selective for centre colour-opponent, UVON-greenOFF stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental validation data.

claim: G28 corresponds to the tSbC RGC type.
source: Therefore, we hypothesised that G28 corresponds to the tSbC RGC type (Tien et al., 2015; Tien et al., 2016; Tien et al., 2022), which is one of the three SbC RGC types identified so far in the mouse and is also referred to as ON delayed (OND) because of its delayed response onset (Jacoby and Schwartz, 2018).
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the response properties and supported by subsequent experimental validation.

claim: tSbC/OND cells exhibited a pronounced selectivity for MEI 28, and were suppressed by most other MEIs.
source: Just like G28 RGCs in the Ca2+ imaging, tSbC/OND cells exhibited a pronounced selectivity for MEI 28, and were suppressed by most other MEIs (Figure 5a, middle and bottom).
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 5a.

claim: The characteristic delayed response onset was visible in both the Ca2+ and electrical responses but was not predicted by the model.
source: Notably, the characteristic delayed response onset was visible in both the Ca2+ (Figure 4f, top) and electrical (Figure 5a) responses but was not predicted by the model (Figure 4f, bottom).
evidence: This is an observation from comparing experimental data to model predictions.

claim: The electrical recordings of the cells' MEI responses yielded virtually the same results as the Ca2+ imaging.
source: Again, the electrical recordings of the cells' MEI responses yielded virtually the same results as the Ca2+ imaging (Figure 5b, middle and bottom; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This validates the Ca2+ imaging approach by comparing it to electrophysiology.

claim: The LN model predicted colour-opponent MEIs for only 9 out of 36 (25%) G28 RGCs.
source: We found that the LN model predicted colour-opponent MEIs for only 9 out of 36 (25%) G28 RGCs (nonlinear CNN: 24 out of 36 [66%] colour-opponent MEIs; Figure 6a–c).
evidence: This is a quantitative comparison between the LN and CNN models.

claim: G28's colour opponency cannot be explained by two opposite-sign linear filters operating on the two colour channels.
source: This finding argues against the possibility that G28's colour opponency can be explained on the computational level by two opposite-sign linear filters operating on the two colour channels, which could be recovered by an LN model.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of LN and CNN model performance.

claim: G28 RGCs have a nonlinear dependency between chromatic contrast (of the stimulus) and chromatic selectivity (of the cell).
source: Instead, it suggests the presence of a nonlinear dependency between chromatic contrast (of the stimulus) and chromatic selectivity (of the cell).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of LN and CNN model performance.

claim: G28 RGCs have a nonlinear tuning for colour contrast: they are strongly UV-selective at lower contrasts, but become colour-opponent (additionally inhibited by green) for higher contrasts.
source: This analysis revealed that, indeed, G28 RGCs have a nonlinear tuning for colour contrast: they are strongly UV-selective at lower contrasts, but become colour-opponent, i.e., additionally inhibited by green, for higher contrasts.
evidence: This is supported by the tuning map analysis shown in Figure 6.

claim: The model's predictions about G28's nonlinear tuning for colour contrast were confirmed using electrical recordings.
source: We confirmed the model's predictions about G28's nonlinear tuning for colour contrast using electrical recordings as described above.
evidence: This is supported by the electrophysiology data shown in Figure 6e-g.

claim: The nonlinearity in tuning to colour contrast of G28 RGCs leads to a transformation of stimulus space that amplifies the distance of colour-opponent stimuli from non-colour-opponent stimuli.
source: The nonlinearity in tuning to colour contrast of G28 RGCs leads to a transformation of stimulus space (Figure 6) that amplifies the distance of colour-opponent stimuli from non-colour-opponent stimuli and is thereby expected to increase their discriminability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the analysis of the tuning maps.

claim: The representation of visual input formed by G28 might serve to detect an ethologically relevant, colour-opponent feature from the visual scene.
source: We therefore hypothesised that the representation of visual input formed by G28 might serve to detect an ethologically relevant, colour-opponent feature from the visual scene.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Chromatic contrast changes at the horizon.
source: Chromatic contrast changes at the horizon (Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Qiu et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2022; Abballe and Asari, 2022)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on natural scene statistics.

claim: Visual context changes at the horizon: from sky to ground or vice versa.
source: Chromatic contrast changes at the horizon (Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Qiu et al., 2021; Gupta et al., 2022; Abballe and Asari, 2022), and so does visual context: from sky to ground or vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited literature and general knowledge.

claim: G28 might leverage chromatic contrast as a proxy for detecting changes in visual context, such as might be caused by head or eye movements that cross the horizon.
source: We therefore hypothesised that G28 might leverage chromatic contrast as a proxy for detecting changes in visual context, such as might be caused by head or eye movements that cross the horizon.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Ground-to-ground and sky-to-sky transitions were distributed along the diagonal in chromatic contrast space, indicating that they reflect largely achromatic contrast changes.
source: We found that ground-to-ground and sky-to-sky transitions were distributed along the diagonal, indicating that they reflect largely achromatic contrast changes.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of inter-clip transitions shown in Figure 7a.

claim: Sky-to-ground transitions fell into the lower right quadrant of chromatic contrast space, and ground-to-sky transitions fell into the upper left quadrant.
source: The two transitions resembling visual input elicited by vertical movements crossing the horizon fell into the two colour-opponent quadrants of the stimulus space: sky-to-ground transitions in the lower right quadrant, and ground-to-sky transitions in the upper left quadrant (Figure 7a and b).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of inter-clip transitions shown in Figure 7a and b.

claim: The UVON-greenOFF MEIs 28 shared a location in stimulus space with ground-to-sky transitions.
source: The UVON-greenOFF MEIs 28, the preferred stimuli of G28, shared a location in stimulus space with ground-to-sky transitions, indicating that these two stimuli are similar in terms of chromatic contrast (Figure 3i).
evidence: This is supported by the comparison of MEI locations and inter-clip transition locations in chromatic contrast space.

claim: G28 RGCs are most strongly tuned to full-field transitions in the upper left quadrant containing mostly ground-to-sky inter-clip transitions.
source: G28 is most strongly tuned to full-field transitions in the upper left quadrant containing mostly ground-to-sky inter-clip transitions (Figure 7c)
evidence: This is supported by the tuning map analysis shown in Figure 7c.

claim: Dorsal G28 (tSbC) RGCs displayed the strongest tuning to ground-to-sky transitions among all dorsal RGCs.
source: We recorded additional fields in the dorsal retina (Figure 7—figure supplement 2) and also found here that G28 (tSbC) RGCs displayed the strongest tuning to ground-to-sky transitions among all dorsal RGCs (Figure 7—figure supplement 3c-h, for statistics, see legends).
evidence: This is supported by the analysis of dorsal retina recordings shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and 3.

claim: G28 RGCs could distinguish ground-to-sky context changes from all other types of transitions robustly across different speeds.
source: This analysis confirmed that G28 RGCs could distinguish ground-to-sky context changes from all other types of transitions robustly across different speeds (Figure 7i and j).
evidence: This is supported by the in silico experiments shown in Figure 7i and j.

claim: The advantage of G28 over other RGC groups in performing the detection task diminished with increasing speed.
source: Interestingly, the advantage of G28 over other RGC groups in performing this detection task diminished with increasing speed (Figure 7—figure supplement 3c and d; see also Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by the in silico experiments shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: A downstream area reading out from a single RGC group would achieve the best performance in detecting ground-to-sky context changes if it based its decisions on inputs from G28 RGCs.
source: Together, these analyses demonstrate that a downstream area, reading out from a single RGC group, would achieve the best performance in detecting ground-to-sky context changes if it based its decisions on inputs from G28 RGCs, robustly across different lighting conditions (transitions between movie snippets), retinal location (ventral and dorsal), and speeds.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the ROC analysis and in silico experiments.

claim: MEIs should not be confused with, or interpreted as, the linear filters derived from classical approaches such as reverse correlation.
source: It is important to note that MEIs should not be confused with, or interpreted as, the linear filters derived from classical approaches such as reverse correlation (Chichilnisky, 2001; Schwartz et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a clarification about the interpretation of MEIs.

claim: The linear filter is optimised to provide the best possible linear approximation of the response function, identifying the stimulus direction to which the cell is most sensitive on average across the stimulus ensemble.
source: The linear filter is optimised to provide the best possible linear approximation of the response function, identifying the stimulus direction to which the cell is most sensitive on average across the stimulus ensemble.
evidence: This describes the properties of linear filters.

claim: The MEI maximises the neuron's response by finding the single stimulus that activates the cell most strongly.
source: In contrast, the MEI maximises the neuron's response by finding the single stimulus that activates the cell most strongly.
evidence: This describes the properties of MEIs.

claim: MEIs can differ significantly from linear filters, often exhibiting greater complexity and higher frequency components.
source: Consequently, MEIs can differ significantly from linear filters, often exhibiting greater complexity and higher frequency components (Walker et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Most previous studies of colour opponency in the mouse retina have identified sparse populations of colour-opponent RGCs that have not been systematically assigned to a particular functional type.
source: Most previous studies of colour opponency in the mouse retina have identified sparse populations of colour-opponent RGCs that have not been systematically assigned to a particular functional type (Szatko et al., 2020; Khani and Gollisch, 2021; Gouras and Ekesten, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Studies that have examined the mechanisms of colour opponency in identified mouse RGC types showed a centre-surround organisation, with RF centre and surround having different chromatic preferences.
source: The only studies that have examined the mechanisms of colour opponency in identified mouse RGC types showed a centre-surround organisation, with RF centre and surround having different chromatic preferences (Chang et al., 2013; Joesch and Meister, 2016; Stabio et al., 2018, but see Sonoda et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: tSbC RGCs respond to spatially co-extensive colour-opponent stimuli, functionally reminiscent of colour-opponent RGCs in guinea pig and ground squirrels.
source: tSbC RGCs, in contrast, respond to spatially co-extensive colour-opponent stimuli, functionally reminiscent of colour-opponent RGCs in guinea pig (Yin et al., 2009) and ground squirrels (Michael, 1968).
evidence: This is supported by the findings of the study and citations to prior research in other species.

claim: It seems unlikely that the opsin gradient plays a major role in the tSbC cell's colour opponency, because both ventral and dorsal tSbC cells preferentially responded to full-field green-to-UV transitions.
source: It seems unlikely, though, that the opsin gradient plays a major role in the tSbC cell's colour opponency, because both ventral and dorsal tSbC cells preferentially responded to full-field green-to-UV transitions.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: In primates, spatially co-extensive colour opponency in small bistratified RGCs is thought to arise from the selective wiring of SON and M/LOFF bipolar cells onto the inner and outer dendritic strata, respectively.
source: In primates, spatially co-extensive colour opponency in small bistratified RGCs is thought to arise from the selective wiring of SON and M/LOFF bipolar cells onto the inner and outer dendritic strata, respectively (Dacey and Lee, 1994, but see Field et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research in primates.

claim: A similar wiring pattern seems unlikely for tSbC RGCs, since their inner dendrites do not co-stratify with the S-ON (type 9) bipolar cells, nor do their outer dendrites co-stratify with the candidate M-OFF bipolar cell (type 1).
source: A similar wiring pattern seems unlikely for tSbC RGCs, since their inner dendrites do not co-stratify with the S-ON (type 9) bipolar cells, nor do their outer dendrites co-stratify with the candidate M-OFF bipolar cell (type 1) (Behrens et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical data and citation to prior research.

claim: The large RF centres of the tSbC cells, extending well beyond their dendritic fields, come from a non-canonical circuit, in which tonic inhibition onto the RGC via GABAB receptors is relieved via serial inhibition from different amacrine cells using GABAC receptors.
source: The large RF centres of the tSbC cells, extending well beyond their dendritic fields, come from a non-canonical circuit, in which tonic inhibition onto the RGC via GABAB receptors is relieved via serial inhibition from different amacrine cells using GABAC receptors (Mani and Schwartz, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: An intriguing possibility is that a colour-selective amacrine cell is part of the circuit supporting chromatically tuned disinhibition in tSbC cells.
source: An intriguing possibility is that a colour-selective amacrine cell is part of this circuit, perhaps supporting chromatically tuned disinhibition in the absence of selective wiring from the aforementioned cone-selective bipolar cells onto the RGC.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Suppressed-by-contrast responses have been recorded along the early visual pathway in dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), superior colliculus (SC), and primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Suppressed-by-contrast responses have been recorded along the early visual pathway in dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), superior colliculus (SC), and primary visual cortex (V1) (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Piscopo et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The function of suppressed-by-contrast responses is still being debated.
source: Suppressed-by-contrast responses have been recorded along the early visual pathway in dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), superior colliculus (SC), and primary visual cortex (V1) (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Piscopo et al., 2013; Ito et al., 2017), with their function still being debated (Masland and Martin, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: In the retina, three types of SbC RGCs have so far been identified, among them the tSbC cell.
source: In the retina, three types of SbC RGCs have so far been identified (reviewed in Jacoby and Schwartz, 2018), among them the tSbC cell (Mani and Schwartz, 2017; Tien et al., 2015; Tien et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The first report of tSbC RGC light responses in mice connected them to the SbC RGCs previously discovered in rabbit, cat, and macaque, and suggested a role in signalling self-generated stimuli, perhaps for saccade suppression.
source: The first report of their light responses in mice connected them to the SbC RGCs previously discovered in rabbit, cat, and macaque, and suggested a role in signalling self-generated stimuli, perhaps for saccade suppression (Tien et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: tSbC RGC projections were traced to areas in SC, v- and dLGN, and nucleus of the optic tract (NOT).
source: Aided by a new intersectional transgenic line to selectively label tSbC RGCs (Tien et al., 2022), their projections were traced to areas in SC, v- and dLGN, and nucleus of the optic tract (NOT).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: It is unclear whether and how tSbC RGCs contribute to gaze stabilisation.
source: The latter stabilises horizontal eye movements; however, as the medial terminal nucleus, which serves stabilisation of vertical eye movements, lacks tSbC innervation, it is unclear whether and how these RGCs contribute to gaze stabilisation.
evidence: This is an inference based on anatomical data cited from prior research.

claim: A retinal study identified the circuit mechanisms responsible for some of the unique spatial and temporal response properties of tSbC cells and suggested a possible role in defocus detection to drive emmetropization in growing eyes and accommodation in adults.
source: A retinal study identified the circuit mechanisms responsible for some of the unique spatial and temporal response properties of tSbC cells and suggested a possible role in defocus detection to drive emmetropization in growing eyes and accommodation in adults (Mani and Schwartz, 2017; Baden et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The different possible functional roles for tSbC RGCs are not mutually exclusive, and might even be complementary in some cases.
source: These different possible functional roles are not mutually exclusive, and might even be complementary in some cases, highlighting the difficulty in assigning single features to distinct RGC types (Schwartz and Swygart, 2020).
evidence: This is a general statement about the complexity of RGC function supported by citation.

claim: The centre colour opponency discovered in tSbC RGCs could serve to enhance their role in defocus detection by adding a directional signal (myopic vs. hyperopic) based on the chromatic aberration of lens and cornea.
source: In particular, the centre colour opponency that we discovered in tSbC RGCs could serve to enhance their role in defocus detection by adding a directional signal (myopic vs. hyperopic) based on the chromatic aberration of lens and cornea (Gawne and Norton, 2020).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings and citation to prior research.

claim: The horizon is a prominent landmark in visual space: it bisects the visual field into two regions, ground and sky.
source: The horizon is a prominent landmark in visual space: it bisects the visual field into two regions, ground and sky.
evidence: This is a general statement about visual space.

claim: In animals like mice, eye motion largely accounts for head movements and keeps the visual field stable with respect to the horizon.
source: This is particularly relevant in animals like mice, where eye motion largely accounts for head movements and keeps the visual field stable with respect to the horizon (Meyer et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Visual stimuli carry different meaning depending on where they occur relative to the horizon, and context-specific processing of visual inputs is necessary for selecting appropriate behavioural responses.
source: Visual stimuli carry different meaning depending on where they occur relative to the horizon, and context-specific processing of visual inputs is necessary for selecting appropriate behavioural responses (reviewed in Evans et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review article.

claim: A looming stimulus above the horizon is likely to be a predator, the appropriate response to which would be avoidance (escape or freezing).
source: For example, it is sensible to assume that a looming stimulus above the horizon is a predator, the appropriate response to which would be avoidance (i.e. escape or freezing).
evidence: This is a logical inference based on ecological considerations.

claim: A looming stimulus below the horizon is more likely to be harmless or even prey.
source: A similar stimulus below the horizon, however, is more likely to be harmless or even prey.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on ecological considerations.

claim: In downstream circuitry, SbC inputs have been found to converge with 'conventional' RGC inputs onto targets in dLGN and NOT.
source: In downstream circuitry, SbC inputs have been found to converge with 'conventional' RGC inputs onto targets in dLGN and NOT
evidence: This is supported by the context and prior research.

claim: Convergence of tSbC axons with tOFF α or W3 axons may allow 'flagging' the activity of these RGCs with their local context (sky/threat or ground/no threat).
source: Such convergence may allow 'flagging' the activity of these RGCs with their local context (sky/threat or ground/no threat).
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: To be behaviourally useful, a context-change-flagging signal needs to be reliable and robust across different stimulus parameters such as illumination level and velocity.
source: Depending on the behaviour that elicits a context change – be it a head or eye movement or locomotion – the parameters of the incoming stimulus, such as illumination level and velocity, may change. To be behaviourally useful, a context-change-flagging signal needs to be reliable and robust across these different stimulus parameters.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the requirements for a functional signal.

claim: tSbC/G28 RGCs were the only type with robustly high performance across different levels of illumination and all simulated speeds.
source: While many slow-ON RGCs achieve high detection performance at higher transition velocities, probably reacting to the increasingly flash-like stimuli, tSbC/G28 RGCs were the only type with robustly high performance across different levels of illumination and all simulated speeds.
evidence: This is supported by the in silico experiments shown in Figure 7.

claim: All imaging experiments were conducted at the University of Tübingen.
source: All imaging experiments were conducted at the University of Tübingen
evidence: This describes where the experiments were performed.

claim: All electrophysiological experiments were conducted at Northwestern University.
source: All electrophysiological experiments were conducted at Northwestern University
evidence: This describes where the experiments were performed.

claim: For all imaging experiments, 4- to 15-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (N=23) of either sex (10 male, 13 female) were used.
source: For all imaging experiments, we used 4- to 15-week-old C57Bl/6J mice (N=23; JAX 000664) of either sex (10 male, 13 female).
evidence: This describes the animals used in the experiments.

claim: For electrophysiology experiments, ChAT-Cre × Ai14 mice on a C57Bl/6J background (N=2, male, aged 27 and 30 weeks) were used.
source: For electrophysiology experiments, we used ChAT-Cre (JAX 006410) × Ai14 (JAX 007914) mice on a C57Bl/6J background (N=2, male, aged 27 and 30 weeks).
evidence: This describes the animals used in the experiments.

claim: The retinae were bulk-electroporated with the fluorescent Ca2+ indicator Oregon-Green BAPTA-1 (OGB-1).
source: Next, the retinae were bulk-electroporated with the fluorescent Ca2+ indicator Oregon-Green BAPTA-1 (OGB-1), as described earlier (Briggman and Euler, 2011).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: A MOM-type two-photon microscope was used for imaging.
source: We used a MOM-type two-photon microscope (designed by W Denk, purchased from Sutter Instruments) (Euler et al., 2009; Euler et al., 2019)
evidence: This describes the equipment used in the experiments.

claim: Image acquisition was performed at 7.8125 Hz.
source: Image acquisition was performed with custom-made software (ScanM by M Müller and TE) running under IGOR Pro 6.3 for Windows (Wavemetrics), taking time-lapsed 64 × 64 pixel image scans (≈ (100 μm)2) at 7.8125 Hz (Figure 1c).
evidence: This describes the experimental parameters.

claim: Ca2+ responses can be related to the spike rate despite the low frame rate.
source: Despite the low frame rate, the Ca2+ responses can be related to the spike rate (Trapani et al., 2023; Román Rosón et al., 2019; Berens et al., 2018; Theis et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The CNN model consisted of two modules, a convolutional core that was shared between all neurons, and a readout that was specific for each neuron.
source: The CNN model consisted of two modules, a convolutional core that was shared between all neurons, and a readout that was specific for each neuron (Klindt et al., 2017).
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: The core module was modelled as a two-layer CNN with 16 feature channels in each layer.
source: The core module was modelled as a two-layer CNN with 16 feature channels in each layer.
evidence: This describes the model architecture.

claim: The network was trained by minimising the Poisson loss.
source: We trained our network by minimising the Poisson loss
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: Early stopping was used on the correlation between predicted and measured neuronal responses on the validation set.
source: Specifically, we used early stopping (Prechelt, 1998) on the correlation between predicted and measured neuronal responses on the validation set, which consisted of 15 out of the 108 movie clips.
evidence: This describes the training procedure.

claim: An ensemble of five models was used for all analyses and MEI generation.
source: For all analyses and MEI generation, we used an ensemble of models as described in Franke et al., 2022. Briefly, we trained five instances of the same model initialised with different random seeds.
evidence: This describes the modeling approach.

claim: MEIs were synthesised using gradient ascent on a randomly initialised, contrast- and range-constrained input.
source: We used gradient ascent on a randomly initialised, contrast- and range-constrained input to find the stimulus that maximised the mean activation of a given model neuron within a short time window (0.66 s; see Methods; Figure 2d).
evidence: This describes the MEI generation procedure.

claim: The optimisation was run for at least 100 iterations, and then stopped when the number of iterations reached 1000, or when it had converged.
source: Optimisation was run for at least 100 iterations, and then stopped when the number of iterations reached 1000, or when it had converged (whichever occurred first).
evidence: This describes the MEI generation procedure.

claim: The spatial component of MEIs was parameterised as a difference-of-Gaussians (DoG).
source: To analyse the MEIs in terms of these properties, we decomposed them into their spatial and temporal components, separately for green and UV, and parameterised the spatial component as a difference-of-Gaussians (DoG) (Gupta et al., 2022) (N=1613 out of 1947, see Methods).
evidence: This describes the MEI analysis procedure.
